title: The five vowels あいうえお
goal: Read and say the five vowel kana, the first step to reading signs at your arrival in Tokyo.

explain.heading: Japanese is spoken in even beats
body: Japanese is counted in short, even beats called morae. Each hiragana you learn is exactly one beat. So あい is two beats (a-i) and いえ is two beats (i-e). Tap the table once for each kana to feel the rhythm.
English tends to stress some syllables and squash others. In Japanese try to give every beat the same length.

explain.heading: The five vowels
body: Every Japanese syllable ends in one of five clear vowels: あ "a" (as in "father"), い "i" (as in "machine"), う "u" (like "moon" but with relaxed lips), え "e" (as in "bed") and お "o" (as in "more", without gliding).
The audio in this app is your device's Japanese text-to-speech voice. It is synthetic, and quality differs from device to device.

explain.heading: About the romaji hints
body: Under each kana you will see romaji (the Latin spelling) as a helper. It is a crutch: the hint fades once a kana is secure, because the goal is to read kana directly.

title: The k row かきくけこ
goal: Add five more kana and read your first colour and body words.

explain.heading: Consonant + vowel
body: The k row is the consonant k followed by each vowel in the same order as before: か ka, き ki, く ku, け ke, こ ko.
Say k lightly, without the puff of air English adds in "kite". The vowel stays pure and short.

explain.heading: Words you can already read
body: With only ten kana you can read adjectives that end in い: あかい (red), あおい (blue) and おおきい (big). Words ending in い that describe things are called i-adjectives; you will study them properly in a later unit.

examples.en: big (the first お is written twice: a long "oo")

title: The s row さしすせそ
goal: Learn the s row, including the special sound し, and read food words you will see in Tokyo.

explain.heading: The s row and the sound "shi"
body: さ sa, し shi, す su, せ se, そ so. Notice し is "shi", not "si": it is pronounced like the start of "sheep". Keyboards usually accept both "shi" and "si" when you type.
The u in す is often very light in everyday speech, so すし sounds close to "ssh-shi". Aim for a short, quiet u.

explain.heading: Little words for places
body: ここ (here), そこ (there, near the listener) and あそこ (over there, far from both of you) form a set. You will use all three at a station.

title: The t row たちつてと
goal: Finish the t row, the two special sounds ち and つ, and start counting.

explain.heading: Two special sounds
body: た ta, ち chi, つ tsu, て te, と to. Two of them change the consonant: ち is "chi" (like "cheese") and つ is "tsu" (the "ts" of "cats" followed by a short u). Do not say "ti" or "tu".

explain.heading: Counting and asking "how many"
body: いち is one and しち is seven. The word いくつ asks "how many?" about things; the answer pattern comes in a later unit.

title: The n row なにぬねの
goal: Complete your first 25 kana, including look-alikes ぬ, ね and の, and read animal and food words.

explain.heading: Five more, and look-alikes
body: な na, に ni, ぬ nu, ね ne, の no. Some kana look alike, such as ぬ and ね: compare them side by side and say the sound aloud each time you see them.
の is also a very common little word that links two nouns; you will see it in phrases like ねこ の て (the cat's paw) in the next lesson.

explain.heading: Where the pitch goes
body: Japanese words have a pitch pattern (high and low tones) rather than strong stress. This course does not teach pitch accent yet; the synthetic voice gives a rough idea, but it is not a reliable model.

title: Words in phrases
goal: Read short phrases built from your 25 kana, as on shop labels and menus.

explain.heading: Spaces and the little words の and と
body: Beginner and children's texts put spaces between words, as in this course. Normal adult text has no spaces; you will meet that soon.
の links two nouns: A の B is "B of A", like 's in English (ねこ の て: the cat's paw). と links two nouns with "and" (いか と たこ: squid and octopus). Treat them as small connecting words for now.

explain.heading: Describing words go first
body: The word that describes a noun comes right before it: おいしい すし (delicious sushi), ちいさい ねこ (a small cat).

title: Listen and read
goal: Tell similar-sounding words apart by ear and read a shop sign and a menu board.

explain.heading: Listening for every beat
body: Many mix-ups come from missing a beat: くち (2 beats) and くつ (2 beats) differ in the last kana, while おと (2 beats) and おとこ (3 beats) differ by length. Count the beats as you listen.
If your device has no Japanese voice, the app shows the transcript instead and says so.

explain.heading: Reading signs
body: Shop labels and menu boards use short phrases: what it is, and what it is like. Find the describing word and the noun, then answer the question.
